items.title: cipherstash Provider
items.text:
Use the CipherStash provider to manage machine identities, ZeroKMS clients, keysets, and keyset grants in a workspace, and to install EQL v4 into PostgreSQL databases. Configure a separate provider instance for each workspace. See the workspace documentation for the CipherStash concepts.

The provider has two optional halves. auth connects to a CipherStash workspace and is required by every CipherStash resource and data source. database connects to a PostgreSQL server and is required by cipherstash_eql_v4. Without auth, the provider never reads CS_* environment variables or contacts CipherStash; without database, it never connects to PostgreSQL.

This provider is in development and is not published to the Terraform Registry. It uses this repository's public pkg/stack/auth and pkg/stack/manage Go packages. Builds require no BNDRY module, sibling SDK checkout, local module replacement or WebAssembly guest. The provider is licensed under the MIT License.

Authenticate with an Admin access key. The provider requires a verified Admin role even for configurations that manage only ZeroKMS resources or read data sources. Successful configuration does not prove permission for every operation. Create this credential outside the Terraform configuration that uses it. Resource access keys and client key values are stored in Terraform state and saved plans, even when marked sensitive. Provider settings are not stored in state, but saved plans can contain them. Protect these files and your state backend.

Neither the provider nor manage.Config reads CS_CLIENT_ID: it identifies an application encryption client, not an authentication principal. Manage client/keyset pairs explicitly with cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant.

items.title: Optional
items.text:
• auth (Attributes) Connection to a CipherStash workspace. Every CipherStash resource and data source requires it. Set it to {} to take both values from the environment. When it is omitted, the provider never reads CS_WORKSPACE_CRN, CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY or CS_CTS_HOST and never contacts CipherStash. When CS_CTS_HOST is set, as in CipherStash's SDKs, the provider sends the access key and management requests to that CipherStash Token Service instead of the workspace region's, and requires it to have issued the tokens. It must be an HTTPS URL, or HTTP to a loopback host, without credentials, query or fragment; an empty value is ignored. (see below for nested schema)
  • database (Attributes) Connection to a PostgreSQL server. cipherstash_eql_v4 requires it and names the database to use. Unset arguments fall back to the libpq environment variables PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGSSLMODE and PGSSLROOTCERT, and to the password file. Connect as a role that can create the ORE operator class: a superuser, or rds_superuser on Amazon RDS and Aurora. The connection opens only when a resource needs it, so these values may be unknown during planning. (see below for nested schema)

items.title: Nested Schema for auth
items.text:
Optional:

  • client_access_key (String, Sensitive) Access key with the Admin role for this workspace. Omit this argument or set it to null to use CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY. Explicit known values override the environment. Empty, unknown or malformed selected values are rejected without fallback. CS_ACCESS_KEY, CS_CONTROL_ACCESS_KEY and CIPHERSTASH_ACCESS_KEY are ignored. Native authentication verifies the token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry, workspace and Admin role before using it. Credentials without Admin, including Control-only and Member-only credentials, are rejected. CipherStash services authorize each request.
  • workspace_crn (String) CipherStash Resource Name (CRN) of the workspace, in the format crn:<region>.aws:<workspace ID>. Omit this argument or set it to null to use CS_WORKSPACE_CRN. Explicit known values override the environment. Empty, unknown or malformed selected values are rejected without fallback; no saved profile is read.

items.title: Nested Schema for database
items.text:
Optional:

  • host (String) Server host name or IP address. Null uses PGHOST.
  • password (String, Sensitive) Password for the role. Null uses PGPASSWORD or the password file.
  • port (Number) Server port. Null uses PGPORT, or 5432.
  • sslmode (String) libpq TLS mode: disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full. Null uses PGSSLMODE, or prefer. Use verify-full outside local development.
  • sslrootcert (String) Path to the certificate authorities that verify the server certificate. Null uses PGSSLROOTCERT.
  • username (String) Role to connect as. Null uses PGUSER. The role that installs EQL owns every EQL object.

items.title: cipherstash_zerokms_client (Data Source)
items.text:
Read an existing ZeroKMS client's name, description, and granted keyset IDs in the configured workspace. Use this data source when your application already has a client and you do not want Terraform to manage it.

This lookup does not import the client, change its grants, or recover its client key value. Removing the data source from your configuration does not delete the client. A missing client or failed lookup returns an error, not an empty result.

items.title: Required
items.text: • id (String) ID of an existing ZeroKMS client in the configured workspace, as a UUID.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text:
• description (String) Current description of the ZeroKMS client.
  • keyset_ids (Set of String) IDs of all keysets granted to the client, including disabled keysets. An empty set means the client has no grants. This lookup does not select a keyset or change any grants.
  • name (String) Current name of the ZeroKMS client.

items.title: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform
items.text:
An application that stores encrypted data with CipherStash needs two things before it can run. It needs credentials for CipherStash's key service, and it needs a PostgreSQL database that understands encrypted values. Setting these up by hand means clicking through the CipherStash Dashboard, copying four secrets into your deployment, and running a 60,000-line SQL script against the database. Nobody can repeat that process exactly, or review it.

The CipherStash Terraform provider does all of it from one configuration file. In this tutorial, you'll use it to set up an imaginary invoices service. You'll give it its own encryption keys and credentials, install CipherStash's encrypted query support into a local PostgreSQL database, and grant the service's database role access to it.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: What you'll build
items.text:
By the end, two commands confirm the setup. The first prints the four environment variables the invoices service needs (values shortened here):

$ terraform output -json app_environment
{"CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY":"CSAKJBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP.6Zq…","CS_CLIENT_ID":"4f8e2a6c-1b3d-4e5f-9a7b-8c6d5e4f3a2b","CS_CLIENT_KEY":"o2FrZXlzZXRf…","CS_WORKSPACE_CRN":"crn:ap-southeast-2.aws:ZVATKW3VHMFG27DY"}

The second connects to the database as the service's own role and asks which version of CipherStash's encrypted query support is installed:

$ docker exec --env PGPASSWORD="${INVOICES_APP_PASSWORD?}" invoices-postgres \
    psql --host=127.0.0.1 --username=invoices_app --dbname=invoices \
    --tuples-only --no-align --command='SELECT eql_v4.version();'
go-0.1.0-rc.4
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: A few terms
items.text:
• CipherStash workspace: your account's isolated space in CipherStash. Its workspace CRN is an identifier such as crn:ap-southeast-2.aws:ZVATKW3VHMFG27DY, which names both the workspace and its region.
  • Access key: a credential, beginning with CSAK, that lets a program talk to CipherStash. Each key has a role. admin can manage the workspace, and member can only encrypt and decrypt.
  • Keyset: a set of encryption keys. Data encrypted under one keyset can't be decrypted with another, so you'd typically use one keyset per application or tenant.
  • Client and client key: an application's half of CipherStash's split-key design. A client can only use the keysets it has been granted.
  • EQL, short for Encrypt Query Language: a set of PostgreSQL types and functions that let the database store, compare and index encrypted values. Version 4 lives in the schemas eql_v4 and eql_v4_internal.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
You need:

  • A CipherStash workspace you can experiment in. The keyset you create in this tutorial can be disabled but not deleted, so don't use a production workspace.
  • An access key for that workspace with the admin role. Create one on the Access Keys page of the CipherStash Dashboard, and copy the workspace CRN shown in the Dashboard. The provider uses the key only to create the other resources. Your application never sees it.
  • Terraform 1.14. This tutorial uses Terraform 1.14.6.
  • Docker, to run PostgreSQL 16.11 locally.
  • Git and mise, to build the provider. The provider isn't in the Terraform Registry yet.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Install the CipherStash provider
items.text:
Build the provider and install it into a local mirror that Terraform can read:

git clone https://github.com/cipherstash/terraform-provider-cipherstash.git && \
  cd terraform-provider-cipherstash && \
  mise trust && \
  mise install && \
  mise run install-local && \
  export TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE="$PWD/.local/terraform.rc" && \
  cd ..

TF_CLI_CONFIG_FILE tells Terraform to load the CipherStash provider from that mirror. Run the remaining steps in the same terminal so the variable stays set.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Set your credentials
items.text:
Set the values that are specific to you. Replace the workspace CRN with your own, and pick a password for the local database. The password can be anything, because the database only runs on your machine.

# Replace with your workspace CRN from the CipherStash Dashboard.
export TF_VAR_workspace_crn='crn:ap-southeast-2.aws:ZVATKW3VHMFG27DY'

# Password for the local PostgreSQL superuser. Any value works.
export PGPASSWORD='mellow-lantern-58'

Then enter your Admin access key without it appearing on screen or in your shell history:

read -r -s -p 'Admin access key: ' CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY && \
  export CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY && \
  echo

The provider reads CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY from the environment, so the key never appears in your configuration files.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Create the invoices service's CipherStash credentials
items.text:
Create a directory for the configuration:

mkdir invoices-infra && cd invoices-infra

Create invoices-infra/main.tf with the following contents:

# invoices-infra/main.tf
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.14.0"

  required_providers {
    cipherstash = {
      source  = "terraform.local/cipherstash/cipherstash"
      version = "0.0.1"
    }
  }
}

variable "workspace_crn" {
  type = string
}

provider "cipherstash" {
  # Connect to CipherStash. The Admin access key comes from CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY.
  auth = {
    workspace_crn = var.workspace_crn
  }
}

# The keys that will encrypt invoice data.
resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset" "invoices" {
  name        = "invoices"
  description = "Customer invoices"
}

# The invoices service's half of the split key.
resource "cipherstash_zerokms_client" "invoices_api" {
  name        = "invoices-api"
  description = "Invoices API service"
}

# Allow the invoices service to use the invoices keyset.
resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant" "invoices_api" {
  client_id = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
  keyset_id = cipherstash_zerokms_keyset.invoices.id
}

# The invoices service's identity and its own access key. The member role
# can encrypt and decrypt, but can't change the workspace.
resource "cipherstash_cts_actor" "invoices_api" {
  name = "invoices-api"
  role = "member"
}

# The four environment variables the invoices service needs.
output "app_environment" {
  sensitive = true
  value = {
    CS_WORKSPACE_CRN     = var.workspace_crn
    CS_CLIENT_ID         = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
    CS_CLIENT_KEY        = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.client_key
    CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY = cipherstash_cts_actor.invoices_api.access_key
  }
}

Initialize Terraform, review the plan, and apply it:

terraform init && \
  terraform plan -out=invoices.tfplan && \
  terraform apply invoices.tfplan

The plan should end with Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. When the apply finishes, print the service's environment:

terraform output -json app_environment

You should see the four CS_* variables from What you'll build. In a real deployment, you'd store these in your secret manager. Terraform also keeps them in its state file, so protect that file too.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Start a local PostgreSQL database
items.text:
Start PostgreSQL 16.11 with a database named invoices, and wait until it accepts connections:

docker run \
  --detach \
  --name invoices-postgres \
  --env POSTGRES_PASSWORD="${PGPASSWORD?}" \
  --env POSTGRES_DB=invoices \
  --publish 5432:5432 \
  postgres:16.11 && \
  until docker exec invoices-postgres \
    pg_isready --host=127.0.0.1 --username=postgres --dbname=invoices --quiet; do
    sleep 1
  done

EQL compares some encrypted values using the pgcrypto extension, so add it to the database's public schema:

docker exec invoices-postgres \
  psql --username=postgres --dbname=invoices --command='CREATE EXTENSION pgcrypto;'

If pgcrypto were missing, the EQL installer would create it in a separate extensions schema, and every database role using encrypted ordering would then need an extra grant on that schema.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Install EQL v4 into the database
items.text:
Replace the contents of invoices-infra/main.tf with the following. Two things change: the provider block gains a database connection, and a new cipherstash_eql_v4 resource installs EQL.

# invoices-infra/main.tf
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.14.0"

  required_providers {
    cipherstash = {
      source  = "terraform.local/cipherstash/cipherstash"
      version = "0.0.1"
    }
  }
}

variable "workspace_crn" {
  type = string
}

provider "cipherstash" {
  # Connect to CipherStash. The Admin access key comes from CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY.
  auth = {
    workspace_crn = var.workspace_crn
  }

  # Connect to PostgreSQL. The password comes from PGPASSWORD.
  database = {
    host     = "localhost"
    port     = 5432
    username = "postgres"
    sslmode  = "disable" # The local container has no TLS. Use "verify-full" in production.
  }
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset" "invoices" {
  name        = "invoices"
  description = "Customer invoices"
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_client" "invoices_api" {
  name        = "invoices-api"
  description = "Invoices API service"
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant" "invoices_api" {
  client_id = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
  keyset_id = cipherstash_zerokms_keyset.invoices.id
}

resource "cipherstash_cts_actor" "invoices_api" {
  name = "invoices-api"
  role = "member"
}

# Install EQL v4 into the invoices database. The provider contains the
# installer for each supported version; this is the version that matches
# release v0.1.0-rc.4 of CipherStash's Go library.
resource "cipherstash_eql_v4" "invoices" {
  database = "invoices"
  version  = "go-0.1.0-rc.4"
}

output "app_environment" {
  sensitive = true
  value = {
    CS_WORKSPACE_CRN     = var.workspace_crn
    CS_CLIENT_ID         = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
    CS_CLIENT_KEY        = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.client_key
    CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY = cipherstash_cts_actor.invoices_api.access_key
  }
}

Apply the change:

terraform plan -out=invoices.tfplan && \
  terraform apply invoices.tfplan

The plan should end with Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. The provider runs the whole installation in one transaction. If anything goes wrong, such as the role lacking permission to create EQL's index support, it rolls back and the database is left unchanged.

Check that EQL is installed:

docker exec invoices-postgres \
  psql --username=postgres --dbname=invoices \
  --tuples-only --no-align --command='SELECT eql_v4.version();'

It should print go-0.1.0-rc.4. To see what EQL adds, create a table with an encrypted column. The public.eql_v4_text_eq type holds an encrypted string that can be compared for equality:

docker exec invoices-postgres \
  psql --username=postgres --dbname=invoices \
  --command='CREATE TABLE invoices (invoice_number bigint PRIMARY KEY, customer_email public.eql_v4_text_eq);'

PostgreSQL prints CREATE TABLE. The invoices service would encrypt each email address with CipherStash before inserting it, so the database only ever stores ciphertext.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Let the invoices service's database role use EQL
items.text:
So far you've used the database superuser. The invoices service should connect as its own role, and that role needs permission to use EQL's two schemas. The CipherStash provider leaves database roles and grants to the community PostgreSQL provider, cyrilgdn/postgresql, which you add in this step.

Pick a password for the service's role:

# Password for the invoices service's database role. Any value works.
export INVOICES_APP_PASSWORD='quiet-harbor-91' && \
  export TF_VAR_invoices_app_password="${INVOICES_APP_PASSWORD?}"

Replace the contents of invoices-infra/main.tf with the following. It adds the PostgreSQL provider, an invoices_app role, and grants on both EQL schemas. This is also the complete example in the provider's repository.

# invoices-infra/main.tf
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.14.0"

  required_providers {
    cipherstash = {
      source  = "terraform.local/cipherstash/cipherstash"
      version = "0.0.1"
    }
    postgresql = {
      source  = "cyrilgdn/postgresql"
      version = "1.27.0"
    }
  }
}

variable "workspace_crn" {
  type = string
}

variable "invoices_app_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}

provider "cipherstash" {
  # Connect to CipherStash. The Admin access key comes from CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY.
  auth = {
    workspace_crn = var.workspace_crn
  }

  # Connect to PostgreSQL. The password comes from PGPASSWORD.
  database = {
    host     = "localhost"
    port     = 5432
    username = "postgres"
    sslmode  = "disable" # The local container has no TLS. Use "verify-full" in production.
  }
}

# The community PostgreSQL provider, for roles and grants. It also reads PGPASSWORD.
provider "postgresql" {
  host     = "localhost"
  port     = 5432
  username = "postgres"
  sslmode  = "disable"
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset" "invoices" {
  name        = "invoices"
  description = "Customer invoices"
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_client" "invoices_api" {
  name        = "invoices-api"
  description = "Invoices API service"
}

resource "cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant" "invoices_api" {
  client_id = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
  keyset_id = cipherstash_zerokms_keyset.invoices.id
}

resource "cipherstash_cts_actor" "invoices_api" {
  name = "invoices-api"
  role = "member"
}

resource "cipherstash_eql_v4" "invoices" {
  database = "invoices"
  version  = "go-0.1.0-rc.4"
}

# The role the invoices service connects as.
resource "postgresql_role" "invoices_app" {
  name     = "invoices_app"
  login    = true
  password = var.invoices_app_password
}

# Let the role use both EQL schemas. EQL's functions run with the caller's
# permissions and reach into eql_v4_internal, so the role needs both.
# Referring to the EQL resource's schema names makes Terraform install EQL
# before granting on its schemas.
resource "postgresql_grant" "invoices_app_eql" {
  for_each = toset([
    cipherstash_eql_v4.invoices.schema,
    cipherstash_eql_v4.invoices.internal_schema,
  ])

  database    = "invoices"
  role        = postgresql_role.invoices_app.name
  schema      = each.key
  object_type = "schema"
  privileges  = ["USAGE"]
}

output "app_environment" {
  sensitive = true
  value = {
    CS_WORKSPACE_CRN     = var.workspace_crn
    CS_CLIENT_ID         = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.id
    CS_CLIENT_KEY        = cipherstash_zerokms_client.invoices_api.client_key
    CS_CLIENT_ACCESS_KEY = cipherstash_cts_actor.invoices_api.access_key
  }
}

Download the new provider and apply:

terraform init && \
  terraform plan -out=invoices.tfplan && \
  terraform apply invoices.tfplan

The plan should end with Plan: 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. The three are the role and one grant for each EQL schema.

Now connect as invoices_app and run the check from What you'll build:

docker exec --env PGPASSWORD="${INVOICES_APP_PASSWORD?}" invoices-postgres \
  psql --host=127.0.0.1 --username=invoices_app --dbname=invoices \
  --tuples-only --no-align --command='SELECT eql_v4.version();'

It should print go-0.1.0-rc.4. Without the grants, the same command fails with permission denied for schema eql_v4.

The invoices service now has everything it needs: the four CS_* variables to reach CipherStash, and a database role that can use EQL. The file from this step is the complete configuration.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: Clean up
items.text:
Destroy everything Terraform created, then remove the container:

terraform destroy -auto-approve && \
  docker rm --force invoices-postgres

Destroying revokes the grants, drops the invoices_app role and uninstalls EQL, which works because no table uses EQL's types. It also deletes the actor, its access key, the client and the keyset grant. The keyset itself can't be deleted, so Terraform disables it and leaves it in your workspace.
path: Prepare CipherStash and PostgreSQL for encrypted data with Terraform

items.title: cipherstash_cts_actor (Resource)
items.text:
Create a machine identity and its access key in the configured workspace. An actor represents an application (app) or agent (agent); it is separate from a ZeroKMS client or a human workspace member.

Changing any argument replaces the actor and creates a new access key. The CipherStash Token Service (CTS) does not support updating actors, and access-key credentials cannot edit access keys. Replacement is not a guarantee that the old credential or its issued tokens stop working immediately. Plan credential changes separately.

The access key is returned only when the actor is created. Terraform stores it in state and saved plans despite marking it sensitive. Import cannot recover the access key or token lifetime.

items.title: Required
items.text: • name (String) Name of the actor and its access key. Use a unique name within the workspace, from 1 to 41 characters. Changing this value replaces the actor.

items.title: Optional
items.text:
• kind (String) Type of machine identity: app or agent. Defaults to app. Changing this value replaces the actor.
  • role (String) Access-key role: admin, control, or member. Defaults to member. Use Member for application cryptographic operations and Control for keyset and client-access automation; Control cannot derive data keys. Changing this value replaces the actor.
  • token_expiry (Number) Lifetime of tokens issued from the access key, in seconds, from 1 to 86400. When omitted, CTS uses 900 seconds. This does not set the access key's lifetime. CipherStash does not return this setting, so Terraform cannot detect changes made outside Terraform; it is null after import. Changing this value replaces the actor.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text:
• access_key (String, Sensitive) Secret access-key value, beginning with CSAK. Returned only at creation and retained in Terraform state; null after import. Marking it sensitive does not remove it from state or saved plans.
  • created_at (String) Creation time reported by CipherStash.
  • id (String) Actor ID, for example app-JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP. Use this ID to import an existing actor.
  • key_id (String) 16-character ID of the actor's access key. This is an identifier, not the secret access-key value.

items.title: cipherstash_eql_v4 (Resource)
items.text:
Install CipherStash EQL v4, the PostgreSQL types and functions that store, compare and index encrypted values, into one database. The provider's database settings choose the server and role; the role that installs EQL owns every EQL object.

The provider contains the installer for each supported version: the eql-v4-install.sql asset of the matching cipherstash/stack Go release, checked against its SHA-256. Create runs it in one transaction with search_path = public, under the same advisory lock as the stash CLI's installer. It refuses, changing nothing, if the database already has an eql_v4 or eql_v4_internal schema (import it instead), if pgcrypto is installed in a schema other than public or extensions, or if the role lacks CREATE on the database or on public. After the installer runs, it rolls back unless eql_v4.version() matches and, when require_ore is true, the ORE operator class exists.

Install pgcrypto before EQL, for example with a postgresql_extension resource that this resource depends on. Otherwise the installer creates it in a new extensions schema, and every role that compares ORE-encrypted values also needs USAGE on that schema.

EQL issues no grants. Roles that query encrypted columns need USAGE on both schema and internal_schema; grant it with another provider, such as postgresql_grant, referencing these attributes so Terraform installs EQL first.

Changing version to a later release upgrades EQL in one transaction under the same lock. The new installer drops and re-creates both schemas, and the provider restores what that removes: the grants on both schemas and their routines and types, the default privileges in them and, when allow_index_rebuild is true, the indexes that call EQL functions, with their comments and CLUSTER marks. It refuses, changing nothing, to move to an earlier release; while any other object outside EQL depends on EQL, such as a view, policy or constraint that calls an EQL function, or an index on a partitioned table, a materialized view or another session's temporary table, in a non-default tablespace or with a statistics target; while indexes need rebuilding and allow_index_rebuild is false; or if the role lacks the privileges of the owner of the EQL objects, of the tables whose indexes it rebuilds, or of the roles whose default privileges it restores. Tables whose indexes it rebuilds are locked until the upgrade commits. Routines and types that are new in the release get what the restored default privileges grant, as if they had been created after them. Restored grants record the database role as grantor. To upgrade from a version this provider does not ship, upgrade by hand as the README describes.

Destroy uninstalls EQL in one transaction under the same lock. It refuses, changing nothing, while any column uses a public.eql_v4_* domain, while any object outside EQL depends on it (such as an index or view that calls an EQL function), if the role lacks the privileges of the owner of the EQL schemas or of the domains and functions EQL adds to public, or if the provider has no uninstaller for the version the database reports, which planning already rejects, before Terraform destroys anything else. Otherwise it runs that release's eql-v4-uninstall.sql, which drops both schemas, then drops the domains and functions it leaves in public, without CASCADE. pgcrypto and the extensions schema stay. To stop managing the installation without changing the database, use a removed block that sets lifecycle { destroy = false }.

items.title: Required
items.text:
• database (String) Name of the database to install EQL into, on the server from the provider's database settings. Changing this value replaces the resource: destroy uninstalls EQL from the old database, under the same refusals as any destroy, and create installs it in the new one.
  • version (String) EQL version to install, as eql_v4.version() reports it, such as go-0.1.0-rc.4 for the installer released with cipherstash/stack Go v0.1.0-rc.4. It must be a version compiled into this provider: go-0.1.0-rc.3, go-0.1.0-rc.4. Refresh reads the installed version, so an installation changed outside Terraform shows as a difference. Changing it to a later version upgrades EQL; changing it to an earlier one is rejected.

items.title: Optional
items.text:
• allow_index_rebuild (Boolean) Whether an upgrade may drop and rebuild the indexes that call EQL functions, which the installer drops. While false, an upgrade refuses when such indexes exist. Defaults to false. Changing it only updates state.
  • require_ore (Boolean) Whether Create rolls back when the installer cannot create the ORE operator class, which needs a superuser or Amazon RDS rds_superuser. Without it the installer disables the 20 ORE-backed domains and still succeeds. Defaults to true. Changing it only updates state.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text:
• id (String) The database name. Use the database name to import an existing installation.
  • internal_schema (String) The schema of EQL's internal functions, eql_v4_internal. Roles that query encrypted columns need USAGE on it as well, because EQL functions run with the caller's privileges.
  • ore_available (Boolean) Whether the ORE operator class exists and no ORE domain is disabled.
  • owner (String) Role that owns schema eql_v4: the role that installed EQL.
  • pgcrypto_schema (String) Schema of the pgcrypto extension, which EQL's ORE comparisons call. Null when pgcrypto is not installed.
  • schema (String) The EQL schema, eql_v4. Reference it in grants so Terraform installs EQL before granting on it.
  • sha256 (String) SHA-256 of the installer for version, matching the release asset. Null after refresh finds a version this provider has no installer for.

items.title: cipherstash_zerokms_client (Resource)
items.text:
Create a ZeroKMS client and its client key in the configured workspace. This is a registered application client, not an SDK encryption-client object. Its client key is the application-held half of CipherStash's split key architecture.

Create does not choose a keyset, so CipherStash creates the workspace's default keyset if needed and grants the new client access to it. CipherStash owns that keyset and grant; you do not need to import or manage either. This resource manages the client identity, not its grants. Use cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant for access to keysets you manage. Refresh and import never change grants or the default keyset, delete removes only the client, and a client remains managed even with no grants. Changing name or description replaces the client and creates a new client key. Existing grants are not transferred to the replacement; plan the credential and grant changes before replacing a client. Creating a replacement does not establish when the old credential stops working.

The client key value is returned only at creation and stored in Terraform state and saved plans despite being marked sensitive. Import by client UUID, whatever grants the client has; import cannot recover the client key, so it is null afterward. Use the cipherstash_zerokms_client data source's keyset_ids for current grant inventory.

items.title: Required
items.text:
• description (String) Description of the ZeroKMS client. Changing this value replaces the client.
  • name (String) Name of the ZeroKMS client. Changing this value replaces the client.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text:
• client_key (String, Sensitive) Secret client key for CS_CLIENT_KEY, returned as base64 at creation. Null after import, because CipherStash returns the key only at creation. Refresh retains it. Sensitive values remain in state and saved plans.
  • id (String) Client ID as a UUID. Use this value for CS_CLIENT_ID in your application.

items.title: cipherstash_zerokms_keyset (Resource)
items.text:
Create and manage a keyset in ZeroKMS. A keyset is an independent authority-key scope: clients must be granted access to use it. This resource manages the keyset's name, description, and enabled status without creating a client or grant. Use cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant to grant access separately.

CipherStash owns the workspace default keyset, which it creates when needed and grants to every new cipherstash_zerokms_client. Do not manage it with this resource: import refuses it, refresh fails while it is in state, and update and destroy check live inventory and refuse to change or disable it. To stop managing it without changing it, use a removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false }.

Changes update the existing keyset without rotating its key material. Destroy disables the keyset and removes it from Terraform state; it does not delete the keyset or its key material. Disabling can interrupt every client using the keyset, but leaves grants in place. Import the retained keyset ID to manage it again.

Give each keyset one owner: Terraform or your provisioning automation, not both. Live Development API probes created, enabled and disabled an isolated test keyset. These probes do not establish the full Terraform lifecycle, including metadata updates; verify that lifecycle before production use. A live test keyset is a lasting resource: this provider can disable it but cannot delete it. See the README's live verification limits.

items.title: Required
items.text:
• description (String) Description of the keyset, from 1 to 256 characters. Changing this value updates the existing keyset.
  • name (String) Name of the keyset, from 1 to 64 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, slashes, or hyphens. Changing this value updates the existing keyset. CipherStash reserves default for the workspace's default keyset.

items.title: Optional
items.text: • enabled (Boolean) Whether the keyset is enabled. Defaults to true. Set to false to disable access without deleting key material or grants. To keep an imported keyset disabled, set this to false in your configuration. A new keyset is created enabled, then disabled in a separate request if this is false. Metadata changes require an enabled keyset: a planned enable happens before metadata updates, and a planned disable happens afterward. Metadata changes to an already-disabled keyset require enabled = true; the provider never temporarily enables a keyset configured to remain disabled.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text: • id (String) Keyset ID as a UUID. Use this ID to import an existing keyset, including one retained after destroy.

items.title: cipherstash_zerokms_keyset_grant (Resource)
items.text:
Grant a ZeroKMS client access to one keyset. This resource manages a single client/keyset pair, not the client's full set of grants. Your application must still select the keyset in its SDK configuration.

Destroy revokes only this grant; it does not delete the client or keyset, or change other grants. Changing either ID replaces the grant without transferring any other grants.

Give each pair one owner. Do not manage it from another Terraform resource, state, or provisioning worker. Import an existing pair rather than creating it again. You do not need this resource for the default-keyset grant a new cipherstash_zerokms_client receives: CipherStash owns that grant. Existing imports of such a pair keep working.

CipherStash refuses to revoke a client's creation grant, the grant to the keyset the client was created with, and returns HTTP 400. Destroying this resource for that pair therefore fails and keeps the pair in state; delete the client instead. Other grants can be revoked. Granting a pair that already exists returns HTTP 409. Full Terraform keyset/grant lifecycle verification and live zero-grant inventory evidence remain outstanding. Inventory absence does not prove immediate credential invalidation. See the README's live verification limits.

items.title: Required
items.text:
• client_id (String) ID of an existing ZeroKMS client, as a lowercase UUID. Changing this value replaces the grant; it does not copy the client's other grants.
  • keyset_id (String) ID of an existing keyset, as a lowercase UUID. Changing this value replaces the grant. A disabled keyset can still have grants; a grant does not enable it.

items.title: Read-Only
items.text: • id (String) Grant ID in the format client UUID/keyset UUID. Use the same format to import an existing grant.
